screens.title: Visualization with rqt_graph, RViz, and rqt
screens.narratorSegment: Visual tools turn logs and buzzwords into clear, actionable insight. In this chapter you will learn how to see your ROS system from three complementary perspectives: the communication topology with rqt_graph, the robot and sensors in 3D with RViz, and real-time numeric traces with rqt_plot. You will also learn to tune running nodes with rqt_reconfigure and capture experiments with rosbag so you can replay them later. These tools change debugging from guesswork into a reproducible process. For example, when a navigation stack behaves oddly, rqt_graph tells you whether the expected nodes are connected, RViz shows where the robot thinks it is, and rqt_plot reveals whether velocity commands are oscillating. Throughout the lesson we use concrete commands you can run locally and a short turtlesim lab to practice recording, plotting, and playback. By the end you will be able to identify missing topic links, match RViz displays to message types, and record a bag file for offline debugging. Which visualization will you use first when a robot goes quiet?

keyIdea.title: Why visualize?
keyIdea.text: Visualization exposes connections, sensor data, and timing so you can diagnose software topology, perception mismatches, and control errors faster than reading logs.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.2 › Visualization Overview
Visualization with rqt_graph, RViz, and rqt
See node-topic connections, inspect 3D sensor data, plot signals, tune parameters, and record runs for replay.
What you'll practice
Open rqt_graph, add RViz displays, plot topics, tune parameters with sliders, and record a bag file to replay later.
Why it matters
Visual debugging reduces time-to-fix. You can prove whether errors are sensor, planner, or wiring issues.
Explore Key Topics
rqt_graph
Visualize node-topic connections and spot missing links or type mismatches.
RViz
Explore 3D sensor data, robot models, and coordinate frames with displays tied to topics.
rosbag
Record runs, replay with original timestamps, and reproduce bugs offline.
Concept Visual
Node
turtle_driver

Quick start
Launch rqt_graph with the rosrun command, add an RViz configuration for your robot, and record a short rosbag as you reproduce the issue.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives focus your practice so you gain practical, demonstrable skills. First, you'll use rqt_graph to inspect the running node-topic graph and diagnose missing connections or mismatched message types. Second, you'll use RViz to load displays such as RobotModel, LaserScan, PointCloud2, Image, and TF to verify how sensors and transforms represent the real world. Third, you'll plot live numeric data with rqt_plot and tune node behavior with rqt_reconfigure so you can iterate without restarting. Finally, you'll record and replay experiments with rosbag for offline debugging and repeatable tests. Each objective is paired with hands-on steps and a small milestone: open rqt_graph and capture a screenshot, add a LaserScan display in RViz and confirm points appear, plot controller setpoint and measured output in rqt_plot, adjust a PID gain with rqt_reconfigure, and record a 30-second bag file then replay it for a subscriber node. These are the practical skills that make visualization a routine part of debugging.

screens.title: Learning Objectives (continued)
screens.narratorSegment: These next objectives connect tools to real tasks so you can prove competency. You will use rqt_reconfigure to adjust parameters such as PID gains without restarting nodes; this matters because iterative tuning is faster when you avoid full restarts, and it prevents losing state during experiments. You will learn rosbag commands to record all topics or a chosen subset, inspect bag contents, and play them back at modified speeds or in a loop; this matters for reproducible tests and offline algorithm development. Lastly, you will combine these tools in a short turtlesim lab: open rqt_graph to verify publishers and subscribers, plot the turtle pose fields with rqt_plot while you drive the turtle, tune any available parameters, record a bag of commands and poses, then replay the bag and verify a subscriber reproduces the trajectory. That end-to-end workflow is the milestone that links visualization to debugging and testing.

screens.title: rqt_graph — Inspecting the node-topic graph
screens.narratorSegment: rqt_graph is the quickest way to understand the wiring of a running ROS system. It draws nodes as ellipses and topics as rectangles, linking publishers to subscribers so you can read the system architecture visually. Start it with the provided command and watch the graph update as nodes come and go. A concrete use case: you expect a localization node to subscribe to a sensor topic but the node is isolated. rqt_graph will show the node present but lacking connections, which indicates either a topic name mismatch or a missing publisher. A common misconception is to assume the node itself is broken; often the problem is naming, namespace, or message-type mismatch. rqt_graph also helps find duplicate publishers or incorrect message types quickly — if two publishers appear for one topic and they have incompatible types, your subscribers will not receive usable messages. Practice tip: hide debug and dead nodes to reduce clutter, group by namespace to see logical components, and save the graph image when reporting a bug. What binding issue would you check first when a node appears but has no incoming edges?

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.2 › rqt_graph
What rqt_graph shows
Nodes, topics, and actions with edges that indicate publishing/subscribing relationships. Use grouping and filters to reduce noise.
Concrete example
If your planner should subscribe to /scan but the planner node shows no incoming link, check topic names, remappings, and message types first.
Common mistake
Assuming a node crash. Often it's a namespace mismatch or a publisher not started yet.
Quick command
rosrun rqt_graph rqt_graph
# or run the full rqt GUI
rqt
Key Takeaway

rqt_graph converts topology questions into visual checks — find missing edges and type conflicts quickly.

Annotated subway map (example view)
Use filters to hide /rosout and dead nodes. Grouping by namespace clarifies logical modules.
Tip
Save the image to include in an issue report to show the exact wiring at failure time.
Check
If two publishers appear on one topic, confirm they use the same message type.

screens.title: RViz — 3D visualization and displays
screens.narratorSegment: RViz is the 3D visualization tool that connects message topics to visual displays so you can see what the robot believes about the world. It uses named displays — RobotModel, LaserScan, PointCloud2, Image, TF, Path, Map, and Marker — each subscribed to a topic and drawn in the 3D scene. A clear example: to see LiDAR points, add a LaserScan display and set its topic to /scan; the points will appear in the XY plane. If nothing appears, the most common issues are choosing the wrong topic, mismatched message type, or an incorrect Fixed Frame in RViz. Fixed Frame defines the coordinate reference for all visuals; set it to a known frame like map or base_link. RViz reads the robot description from /robot_description for RobotModel displays, so ensure the parameter is set. Misconception alert: RViz does not publish data — it only subscribes and displays. Use RViz to validate transforms, sensor alignment, and expected geometry before trusting higher-level planners. Try loading a saved. rviz config to reproduce the same visualization across sessions. RViz — 3D visualization and displays means rviz turns messages and tf into a 3d scene so you can verify sensor alignment, robot pose, and planned paths.. In practical terms, map messages to visual displays to inspect pose, sensors, and maps.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.2 › RViz
Common RViz displays
RobotModel, LaserScan, PointCloud2, Image, TF, Path, Map, and Marker — each needs the correct topic and frame.
RobotModel
Uses /robot_description to render links and joints so you can check kinematics and meshes.
LaserScan
Displays 2D LiDAR points. Set topic to /scan and verify the message type matches sensor output.
PointCloud2
Shows 3D point clouds from depth cameras and LiDAR; use RGB or intensity rendering to inspect data quality.
TF
Displays coordinate frames so you can confirm transforms and fixed-frame alignment.
Example command
rosrun rviz rviz
# or start with a saved config
rosrun rviz rviz -d $(find my_package)/rviz/config.rviz
Key Takeaway

Set the Fixed Frame correctly and match topics to display types; RViz is a read-only visualizer for verification.

Common mistake

Nothing appears because the Fixed Frame is invalid or the topic name does not match the display type.

RViz checklist
  • Confirm topic exists with rostopic list and rostopic type.
  • Set Fixed Frame to map, world, or base_link as appropriate.
  • Ensure /robot_description is available for RobotModel.
  • Use Marker displays for custom debugging shapes and text.

screens.title: RViz displays and troubleshooting
screens.narratorSegment: Working with RViz is a small process you can master in three steps: add the right display, point it to the correct topic, and confirm frames match. Start by adding a display type that matches your message: LaserScan for 2D LiDAR, PointCloud2 for 3D clouds, Image for camera streams, and RobotModel for URDF. Next, set the display's Topic field to the exact topic name; verify the correct message type with rostopic type. Finally, check the Fixed Frame and the TF tree so the display can place visuals correctly. A concrete example: to visualize a depth camera, add an Image display and set the topic to /camera/image_raw; then add a PointCloud2 display for the depth cloud topic. If points are floating far away, the likely cause is a TF error or wrong frame_id in the messages. A frequent misconception is thinking RViz modifies data; it only subscribes. For troubleshooting, use rostopic echo to inspect headers and frame_ids and run rostopic type to confirm message formats. This three-step loop — pick, point, verify — will make RViz a fast verification tool. RViz displays and troubleshooting means add the correct display, set the topic, and verify frames and message types to avoid empty or misplaced visuals.. In practical terms, select displays, set topics and frames, then verify the output.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.2 › RViz Workflow
Three steps
1. Add display
Choose a display that matches the message type you want to visualize.
2. Set topic
Point the display to the exact topic name; verify with rostopic list and rostopic type.
3. Verify frames
Confirm Fixed Frame and TF so visuals are placed with correct transforms.
Check your work
If objects seem offset, inspect message header.frame_id and TF to find frame mismatches.
Concrete example
Visualize a LiDAR: add LaserScan display, set topic to /scan, confirm Fixed Frame is base_link or map depending on your setup. If no points appear, confirm the publisher is active with rostopic list and check message types.
Quick checks
  • rostopic list and rostopic type to validate topics.
  • rostopic echo to inspect header.frame_id values.
  • Adjust Fixed Frame until TF error clears.

screens.title: rqt_plot — Live plotting for tuning and debugging
screens.narratorSegment: rqt_plot is a simple but powerful real-time plotting tool. It graphs numeric fields from topics so you can compare setpoints, measurements, and other signals side-by-side. A common use is controller tuning: plot the desired velocity and the measured velocity on the same axes to observe tracking error and oscillations. Start rqt_plot with the command and provide one or more field paths; you can plot nested fields such as sensor_data/temperature. For a concrete example, when debugging a mobile base that oscillates, open rqt_plot with /cmd_vel/linear/x and /cmd_vel/angular/z to see spikes or oscillatory patterns. One misconception is expecting rqt_plot to decode complex structures automatically — you must specify the field path correctly. If you see flat lines, the field path is likely wrong. Use rostopic echo to inspect message structure before plotting. When tuning, make small parameter changes and watch the plot update; this direct feedback loop helps you converge to stable gains more quickly than trial-and-error restarts. rqt_plot — Live plotting for tuning and debugging means rqt_plot makes controller and sensor behaviors visible over time so you can identify spikes, offsets, and oscillations.. In practical terms, plot fields over time to inspect controller behavior and sensor signals.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.2 › rqt_plot
Plotting fields
Specify one or more field paths to visualize numeric time-series from topics.
# Plot a single field
rosrun rqt_plot rqt_plot /topic/field

# Plot multiple fields
rosrun rqt_plot rqt_plot /cmd_vel/linear/x /cmd_vel/angular/z

# Plot nested field
rosrun rqt_plot rqt_plot /sensor_data/temperature
Concrete example
Plot setpoint and measured velocity to see tracking error and oscillations while you adjust gains.
Common mistake

Flat lines usually mean the field path is incorrect or the publisher is inactive. Inspect messages with rostopic echo first.

When to use rqt_plot
  • Tuning controllers (compare setpoint vs measured).
  • Inspecting sensor noise and drift.
  • Validating command rates and spikes during behavior tests.
Tip
Add only the fields you need to reduce visual clutter. Use short recordings with rosbag for replayable plots.

screens.title: rqt_reconfigure — Tune parameters at runtime
screens.narratorSegment: rqt_reconfigure gives you a GUI for dynamically adjustable parameters when a node uses dynamic_reconfigure. This is particularly useful for control gains, thresholds, and behavior flags that need fine-tuning. The interactive slider model allows you to change values and immediately observe effects in RViz or rqt_plot. A concrete example: while tuning a PID controller, slide the proportional gain and immediately observe whether oscillations reduce on your rqt_plot traces. A common misconception is that rqt_reconfigure will change any parameter; the node must expose parameters via dynamic_reconfigure. Also, remember that some changes may not be safe to make on a physical system; start with simulation or low-power tests. For repeatability, record parameter values you used after you achieve a stable behavior, and consider persisting them as ROS parameters or in a launch file. Live tuning speeds iteration because you keep node state and avoid long restart cycles, but always validate changes with controlled tests. rqt_reconfigure — Tune parameters at runtime means use rqt_reconfigure to change exposed parameters live and watch their immediate effect to speed tuning cycles.. In practical terms, change node parameters live to iterate quickly without restarts.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.2 › rqt_reconfigure
What rqt_reconfigure does
Provides sliders and inputs to change parameters exposed via dynamic_reconfigure on running nodes.
Concrete example
Adjust PID proportional gain live while watching rqt_plot to reduce overshoot and oscillation.
Safety note

On hardware, make small steps and validate each change. Not all parameters are safe to modify at full ranges.

Quick command
rosrun rqt_reconfigure rqt_reconfigure
Checklist
  • Ensure the node supports dynamic_reconfigure.
  • Make incremental changes and observe effects in RViz or rqt_plot.
  • Record tuned values for reproducibility.

screens.title: rosbag — Recording and playback workflow
screens.narratorSegment: rosbag is a recording tool that captures topic messages with their timestamps so you can replay them later. Typical workflow: record a subset of topics while reproducing the issue, use rosbag info to inspect the contents, and play back the bag to feed recorded messages into subscribers. For example, record camera and laser topics during a failure so you can reproduce perception problems offline. Commands include recording all topics or chosen topics, providing an output filename, listing bag contents, and playing back with speed adjustments or looping. A common pitfall is clock desynchronization between systems; if playback timing looks wrong on a different machine, use the simulated clock option to force consistent timestamps. When you play a bag file, messages are published with the original timestamps unless you remap or alter timing. Practically, use rosbag to create regression tests, collect datasets for learning, and demonstrate behaviors without the robot present. After recording, replay and verify the same issue occurs with your subscribers — that confirms the problem is not hardware-only. rosbag — Recording and playback workflow means record and replay topic streams to reproduce bugs, run tests, and collect datasets for offline analysis.. In practical terms, capture topics for later replay, debugging, and testing.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Lab steps
  1. Launch turtlesim and open rqt_graph. Hide dead nodes and save a screenshot.

Use RViz when you need to inspect robot pose, TF frames, sensor point clouds, or maps visually in 3D. Use rqt_plot to inspect numeric signals and trends for tuning and stability checks. Use rqt_reconfigure to adjust parameters on nodes that expose dynamic configuration without restarting. Use rosbag to capture and replay topic streams for offline debugging and testing. screens.title: Debugging a navigation fault — a worked example
screens.narratorSegment: Imagine a navigation algorithm that issues erratic velocity commands. Start by plotting the commanded linear and angular velocities with rqt_plot to confirm oscillations or spikes. If you see large spikes, suspect the planner or sensor noise; if you see steady offset, suspect bias. Next, open rqt_graph to ensure the planner, controller, and odometry publishers/subscribers are connected as expected — a missing subscription would explain no corrective action. Use RViz to visualize the robot pose and the map to understand whether perception or localization is drifting. If the sensor data looks noisy, record the relevant sensor topics and cmd_vel to a bag. Play back the bag and feed it to the controller-only stack to determine whether the controller produces the same erratic commands when sensor input is fixed. A frequent misconception is to blame the controller first; often the upstream planner or sensor is the culprit. The full process — observe signals, inspect topology, validate 3D state, record, and replay — helps you separate hardware faults from software bugs and proves the root cause reproducibly. Module 7 › Chapter 6.2 › Debugging Scenario
Step-by-step
1. Plot commands
Use rqt_plot to graph /cmd_vel/linear/x and /cmd_vel/angular/z and look for spikes or oscillation.
2. Inspect topology
Open rqt_graph to confirm planner, controller, and odometry nodes are connected correctly.
3. Visualize state

Example commands

screens.title: Common mistakes and troubleshooting checklist
screens.narratorSegment: When visuals fail or look incorrect, a short checklist quickly narrows the cause. First, confirm the topic exists using rostopic list and inspect its type with rostopic type. Second, check message headers with rostopic echo to ensure frame_id and timestamps are set correctly. Third, verify RViz Fixed Frame and the TF tree so displays can be anchored. Fourth, in rqt_graph confirm nodes are present and connected; a node with no incoming edges usually indicates a naming or remapping issue. Fifth, for rqt_plot ensure you pointed to the correct field path; flat lines usually mean a wrong field. For rosbag playback issues, consider clock differences; use the simulated clock option or match system clocks. A common misconception is blaming the visualization tool; usually the underlying messages or TF are inconsistent. Keep a minimal reproduction: fewer topics and a short bag so you can isolate the problem. This checklist reduces hunting time and helps you communicate clear, reproducible bug reports. 1. Topic & type
rostopic list and rostopic type to confirm the topic name and message format.

Use rostopic echo and check header.frame_id and timestamp fields.

Reduce to essential topics and short bag files to reproduce the problem reliably.

fullNarratorScript:
Visual tools turn logs and buzzwords into clear, actionable insight. In this chapter you will learn how to see your ROS system from three complementary perspectives: the communication topology with rqt_graph, the robot and sensors in 3D with RViz, and real-time numeric traces with rqt_plot. You will also learn to tune running nodes with rqt_reconfigure and capture experiments with rosbag so you can replay them later. These tools change debugging from guesswork into a reproducible process. For example, when a navigation stack behaves oddly, rqt_graph tells you whether the expected nodes are connected, RViz shows where the robot thinks it is, and rqt_plot reveals whether velocity commands are oscillating. Throughout the lesson we use concrete commands you can run locally and a short turtlesim lab to practice recording, plotting, and playback. By the end you will be able to identify missing topic links, match RViz displays to message types, and record a bag file for offline debugging. Which visualization will you use first when a robot goes quiet?

These objectives focus your practice so you gain practical, demonstrable skills. First, you'll use rqt_graph to inspect the running node-topic graph and diagnose missing connections or mismatched message types. Second, you'll use RViz to load displays such as RobotModel, LaserScan, PointCloud2, Image, and TF to verify how sensors and transforms represent the real world. Third, you'll plot live numeric data with rqt_plot and tune node behavior with rqt_reconfigure so you can iterate without restarting. Finally, you'll record and replay experiments with rosbag for offline debugging and repeatable tests. Each objective is paired with hands-on steps and a small milestone: open rqt_graph and capture a screenshot, add a LaserScan display in RViz and confirm points appear, plot controller setpoint and measured output in rqt_plot, adjust a PID gain with rqt_reconfigure, and record a 30-second bag file then replay it for a subscriber node. These are the practical skills that make visualization a routine part of debugging.

These next objectives connect tools to real tasks so you can prove competency. You will use rqt_reconfigure to adjust parameters such as PID gains without restarting nodes; this matters because iterative tuning is faster when you avoid full restarts, and it prevents losing state during experiments. You will learn rosbag commands to record all topics or a chosen subset, inspect bag contents, and play them back at modified speeds or in a loop; this matters for reproducible tests and offline algorithm development. Lastly, you will combine these tools in a short turtlesim lab: open rqt_graph to verify publishers and subscribers, plot the turtle pose fields with rqt_plot while you drive the turtle, tune any available parameters, record a bag of commands and poses, then replay the bag and verify a subscriber reproduces the trajectory. That end-to-end workflow is the milestone that links visualization to debugging and testing.

rqt_graph is the quickest way to understand the wiring of a running ROS system. It draws nodes as ellipses and topics as rectangles, linking publishers to subscribers so you can read the system architecture visually. Start it with the provided command and watch the graph update as nodes come and go. A concrete use case: you expect a localization node to subscribe to a sensor topic but the node is isolated. rqt_graph will show the node present but lacking connections, which indicates either a topic name mismatch or a missing publisher. A common misconception is to assume the node itself is broken; often the problem is naming, namespace, or message-type mismatch. rqt_graph also helps find duplicate publishers or incorrect message types quickly — if two publishers appear for one topic and they have incompatible types, your subscribers will not receive usable messages. Practice tip: hide debug and dead nodes to reduce clutter, group by namespace to see logical components, and save the graph image when reporting a bug. What binding issue would you check first when a node appears but has no incoming edges?

RViz is the 3D visualization tool that connects message topics to visual displays so you can see what the robot believes about the world. It uses named displays — RobotModel, LaserScan, PointCloud2, Image, TF, Path, Map, and Marker — each subscribed to a topic and drawn in the 3D scene. A clear example: to see LiDAR points, add a LaserScan display and set its topic to /scan; the points will appear in the XY plane. If nothing appears, the most common issues are choosing the wrong topic, mismatched message type, or an incorrect Fixed Frame in RViz. Fixed Frame defines the coordinate reference for all visuals; set it to a known frame like map or base_link. RViz reads the robot description from /robot_description for RobotModel displays, so ensure the parameter is set. Misconception alert: RViz does not publish data — it only subscribes and displays. Use RViz to validate transforms, sensor alignment, and expected geometry before trusting higher-level planners. Try loading a saved. rviz config to reproduce the same visualization across sessions. RViz — 3D visualization and displays means rviz turns messages and tf into a 3d scene so you can verify sensor alignment, robot pose, and planned paths.. In practical terms, map messages to visual displays to inspect pose, sensors, and maps.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Working with RViz is a small process you can master in three steps: add the right display, point it to the correct topic, and confirm frames match. Start by adding a display type that matches your message: LaserScan for 2D LiDAR, PointCloud2 for 3D clouds, Image for camera streams, and RobotModel for URDF. Next, set the display's Topic field to the exact topic name; verify the correct message type with rostopic type. Finally, check the Fixed Frame and the TF tree so the display can place visuals correctly. A concrete example: to visualize a depth camera, add an Image display and set the topic to /camera/image_raw; then add a PointCloud2 display for the depth cloud topic. If points are floating far away, the likely cause is a TF error or wrong frame_id in the messages. A frequent misconception is thinking RViz modifies data; it only subscribes. For troubleshooting, use rostopic echo to inspect headers and frame_ids and run rostopic type to confirm message formats. This three-step loop — pick, point, verify — will make RViz a fast verification tool. RViz displays and troubleshooting means add the correct display, set the topic, and verify frames and message types to avoid empty or misplaced visuals.. In practical terms, select displays, set topics and frames, then verify the output.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

rqt_plot is a simple but powerful real-time plotting tool. It graphs numeric fields from topics so you can compare setpoints, measurements, and other signals side-by-side. A common use is controller tuning: plot the desired velocity and the measured velocity on the same axes to observe tracking error and oscillations. Start rqt_plot with the command and provide one or more field paths; you can plot nested fields such as sensor_data/temperature. For a concrete example, when debugging a mobile base that oscillates, open rqt_plot with /cmd_vel/linear/x and /cmd_vel/angular/z to see spikes or oscillatory patterns. One misconception is expecting rqt_plot to decode complex structures automatically — you must specify the field path correctly. If you see flat lines, the field path is likely wrong. Use rostopic echo to inspect message structure before plotting. When tuning, make small parameter changes and watch the plot update; this direct feedback loop helps you converge to stable gains more quickly than trial-and-error restarts. rqt_plot — Live plotting for tuning and debugging means rqt_plot makes controller and sensor behaviors visible over time so you can identify spikes, offsets, and oscillations.. In practical terms, plot fields over time to inspect controller behavior and sensor signals.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

rqt_reconfigure gives you a GUI for dynamically adjustable parameters when a node uses dynamic_reconfigure. This is particularly useful for control gains, thresholds, and behavior flags that need fine-tuning. The interactive slider model allows you to change values and immediately observe effects in RViz or rqt_plot. A concrete example: while tuning a PID controller, slide the proportional gain and immediately observe whether oscillations reduce on your rqt_plot traces. A common misconception is that rqt_reconfigure will change any parameter; the node must expose parameters via dynamic_reconfigure.
